newsitem.title: USA: White House contest shaken by call to muzzle Perot.
newsitem.headline: White House contest shaken by call to muzzle Perot.

text.p: The U.S. presidential race took a new twist on Tuesday when organisers proposed excluding Ross Perot from campaign debates, giving Republican Bob Dole the clear shot he wants at President Bill Clinton.

The proposal by the bipartisan Commission on Presidential Debates drew cheers from Dole's camp, opposition from Clinton backers and fury from Perot partisans, who said they would sue and called this an establishment attempt to muzzle the cantankerous billionaire and Reform Party nominee.

The commission's recommendation, which could be vetoed by the Clinton campaign, was something of a bombshell because it would exclude a high-profile political maverick who cut a strong figure in the 1992 presidential debates and won nearly 19 percent of the popular vote.
The panel said he should be excluded this year because, with only single-digit poll support at present, he no longer had "a realistic chance" of being elected U.S. president.
Later, negotiating teams from the Clinton and Dole campaigns met but failed to agree on the format of the debates and decided to continue the negotiations on Wednesday.

Dole's chief negotiator, former South Carolina Gov. Carroll Campbell, said: "We're probably a few days away from having exactly the format and times and things that are necessary but I think everybody understands that we want to have a debate."

Dole, struggling badly in the polls, wants three or four debates and he wants them to start next week, as originally scheduled. But after Tuesday's meeting, Campbell said a debate next week appeared unlikely.
"I do not think that the schedule of the president will allow a debate next week," Campbell told reporters.

Trade Secretary Micky Kantor, leading the negotiations for Clinton, said his side wanted to hold three presidential and one vice presidential debate all between Oct. 6 and 13. He said he was still pressing for Perot to be included.

In Phoenix, Arizona, where he was pushing his campaign as the superior anti-crime candidate, Dole said he was all the more anxious to face Clinton in the televised forums as soon as possible, and also claimed he would carry Perot's banner.
"I want to reach out to the Perot supporters ... I think we (Republicans) are the Reform party," said Dole, now lagging eight to 16 points behind Clinton in nationwide polls.
Dole strategists wanted Perot out because they assumed he would siphon off more Republican than Democratic votes -- even though independent analysis casts some doubt on that view.
The Dole camp exulted in the news.

"It's become abundantly clear that one of two men will be in the White House next January ... and this makes it a hell of a lot more likely that it's going to be Bob Dole," said Dole adviser Nelson Warfield. "A one-on-one shot with (Clinton) gives us the opportunity to point out the glaring gaps between Clinton's centrist rhetoric and his liberal record."
Clinton advisers said, in effect, not so fast.
Kantor is pressing for two hour-long debates including Perot and his running mate, Pat Choate, with a third and final debate in "town meeting" format to feature only Dole and Clinton.
"We believe that (Perot's) participation is in the public interest," Kantor said before the negotiating session.
Clinton took a breezier approach, positioning himself as the easy-going frontrunner happy to debate all comers including Perot -- and leaving the infighting to underlings.

"I enjoyed having him in there in '92. I thought he made a valuable contribution ... I'm not afraid of any debate," Clinton said during a campaign stop in Westland, Michigan, the first stop in a four-day swing through the Midwest and West.

In 1992 Perot took part in all three presidential campaign debates, peppering then-President George Bush in particular with barbs on his alleged failures of leadership and portraying Bush as an exemplar of an establishment corrupted by special interest influence and money.

Polls showed many voters thought Perot won the first three-way debate. He eventually won a bigger slice of the popular vote than any third-party candidate since Teddy Roosevelt, 80 years earlier in 1912.
This year, running as nominee of his own Reform Party along with running mate Choate, an economist, he has yet to establish a similar appeal which proved to be his undoing.

"Our decision ... was made on the basis that only President Clinton and Senator Dole have a realistic chance as set forth in our criteria to be elected the next president of the United States," the debate commission said.
Its decision could be reconsidered for later debates -- three or four are in prospect -- if Perot grew stronger.
His supporters called the decision "a travesty" typical of the political culture Perot was trying to reform.
"We will file suit in federal court this week" to overturn the exclusion, Perot spokesman Russell Verney said.
